title: Cavity magnonics and bound states in the continuum with Bragg and anti-Bragg mirrors
authors: B. -Y. Wu, K. -P. Li, G. Chen, W. -M. Zhou, C. -X. Run, K. -M. Hsieh, A. F. Kockum, Z. -R. Lin, W. Nie, I. -C. Hoi
abstract: A periodic resonant emitter array coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide can act as a mirror. A typical example is a Bragg mirror, where emitters are spaced by multiples of half wavelengths and collectively enhance light reflection. Two such mirrors form an effective cavity that hosts bound states in the continuum (BICs). However, generating and detecting the spatial profiles of such BICs has proven challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate BICs in cavity magnonics using two periodic ferrimagnetic-sphere arrays and a probe sphere in a dual-open-waveguide architecture. We realize both Bragg and anti-Bragg cavities, whose mirrors have different lattice constants. In the Bragg cavity, there are degenerate supermodes formed by mirror spheres. We show that a single dark supermode coherently couples to the probe magnon in the cavity region, forming two polaritons whose splitting scales with both the probe-sphere size and the number of mirror spheres. By contrast, the anti-Bragg cavity has bright and dark supermodes in a bandgap, substantially changing the magnon-cavity interaction. Moreover, by moving the probe sphere, we perform position-dependent detection of the cavity field, highlighting the role of BICs in these cavities. Our flexible experimental setup with a scanning probe opens possibilities to detect other exotic states created by light-matter interaction, to interface with superconducting circuits in hybrid quantum networks, and to study non-Hermitian physics with Bragg and anti-Bragg cavities.
summary: This paper reports experimental realization of magnonic cavities using periodic arrays of ferrimagnetic spheres acting as Bragg and anti-Bragg mirrors. By measuring waveguide transmission, the authors demonstrate distinct coupling regimes in these two types of cavities. The work highlights the utility of these systems for studying BICs and developing flexible platforms for quantum light-matter interactions.
main_problem: The paper aims to experimentally demonstrate and study Bound States in the Continuum (BICs) within the context of cavity magnonics using engineered magnetic mirrors.
main_result: The authors successfully realized both Bragg and anti-Bragg cavities, showing that the anti-Bragg cavity exhibits a distinct magnon-cavity interaction, including the observation of dissipative coupling signatures.
method: The study uses a dual-open-waveguide architecture with periodic arrays of ferrimagnetic-sphere magnonic mirrors and employs waveguide transmission spectroscopy, supplemented by scanning the probe position.
model_or_system: The system involves magnons in YIG sphere arrays acting as mirrors, coupled to a probe magnon and a transverse waveguide. The physics is modeled using an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian describing coherent and dissipative magnon interactions.
key_observables: Waveguide transmission spectra (|S21|, |S43|), polariton splitting, and the depth of transmission dips as a function of mirror arrangement (Bragg vs. anti-Bragg).
important_parameters: Mirror spacing (Bragg: $n\lambda_0/2$; Anti-Bragg: $3\lambda_0/4$), probe sphere size, and the number of mirror spheres ($N$).
main_assumptions: The deepening of transmission dips in the anti-Bragg cavity is interpreted as evidence of dissipative coupling, rather than simple geometrical interference.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup, energy level diagrams for supermodes, and measured transmission spectra comparing Bragg and anti-Bragg cavity responses.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the theoretical description of the effective Hamiltonian, details the experimental realization of Bragg and anti-Bragg cavities, presents spectroscopic measurements to characterize supermodes and BIC signatures, and concludes by discussing the implications for flexible quantum interfacing.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it uses magnonics (a solid-state analogue to photonics) to explore fundamental concepts like BICs and strong light-matter coupling, mirroring techniques used in cavity QED with atoms.
